name: The Principle of Sufficient Reason
statement: Nothing is so without a reason: everything that is has a sufficient reason why it is so.
statementAccent: everything that is has a sufficient reason why it is so
meaning: The principle of sufficient reason holds that everything must have a reason, cause, or ground: nothing exists, happens, or is the case without a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise. Formally, for every fact there must be a sufficient reason why that fact obtains. The principle demands thoroughgoing intelligibility and rejects brute, unexplainable facts, insisting that in principle an explanation is always available even where we do not know it. It is most strongly associated with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who coined the phrase and made it, together with the principle of contradiction, one of the two great principles of his philosophy, though the idea has antecedents in earlier thinkers including Anaximander, Parmenides, and Spinoza. Arthur Schopenhauer later devoted a whole work, On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason, to distinguishing its different forms. The principle sits at the foundation of rationalist metaphysics and the philosophy of explanation.
mechanism: As a governing principle of reasoning, the principle of sufficient reason functions as a demand that every truth be groundable. Leibniz divided truths into two kinds and matched each to one of his two great principles: necessary truths, such as those of mathematics, rest on the principle of contradiction and hold in all possible worlds; contingent truths, the truths of fact about this world, rest on the principle of sufficient reason, which requires a reason why things are this way rather than another. Applied to the whole of contingent reality, the principle drives Leibniz's version of the cosmological argument: if every contingent being has its reason in another, the entire series of contingent beings still lacks a sufficient reason within itself, so the ultimate explanation must lie in a necessary being, which he identifies with God. Schopenhauer's fourfold root then distinguishes different modes in which the principle operates, the reasons of becoming (causality), of knowing (grounds of judgment), of being (relations in space and time), and of acting (motivation), arguing that confusing these forms is a source of philosophical error.

examples.text: If a ball rests on one side of a table rather than the other, the principle insists there must be some sufficient reason why it is there and not elsewhere.
Leibniz argued the whole series of contingent things needs a reason outside itself, leading to a necessary being as the ultimate explanation.
He distinguished reasons of becoming, knowing, being, and acting, holding that mixing up these forms breeds confusion.

variants.name: The two great principles
variants.text: Leibniz's pairing of the principle of contradiction, governing necessary truths, with the principle of sufficient reason, governing contingent truths of fact.

variants.name: The fourfold root
variants.text: Schopenhauer's division of the principle into four forms: reasons of becoming, knowing, being, and acting.

whyItMatters: The principle of sufficient reason is one of the load-bearing assumptions of rationalist philosophy and of the very project of explanation. If accepted in full, it implies that reality is thoroughly intelligible, that there are no ultimately inexplicable brute facts, and this drives major arguments in metaphysics, from Leibniz's cosmological proof of God to accounts of causation and determinism. It also frames enduring debates: whether the demand for a reason for everything is defensible, and what follows if it is. The principle's tensions are as instructive as its uses. Pressed hard, it threatens to collapse contingency into necessity, the necessitarian worry that if everything has a sufficient reason, everything is ultimately necessary, a road Spinoza embraced. Modern physics raises the sharpest challenge, since quantum mechanics appears to permit events, such as the timing of radioactive decay, without a fully determining prior cause. Whether the principle is true or must be qualified remains a live and central question.

limits: The principle of sufficient reason is a contested philosophical thesis, not an established fact, and it faces serious challenges. Applied to itself, it invites the awkward question of what the sufficient reason for the principle is, a potential self-refutation. Pressed to its limit it courts necessitarianism, the conclusion that if every fact has a sufficient reason then no fact could have been otherwise, eliminating genuine contingency. Modern physics supplies the most concrete difficulty: quantum indeterminacy suggests some events, like when a given radioactive atom decays, lack a fully determining sufficient cause, though interpretations of quantum theory differ. Contemporary philosophers are divided, with some, like Peter van Inwagen, questioning the principle and others, like Alexander Pruss, defending it. So the principle is a powerful and historically central idea about the intelligibility of the world, but its universal truth is genuinely debated rather than settled.
misreadings: The principle of sufficient reason is not a proven law of nature but a philosophical principle that is actively debated and, on some readings, in tension with quantum physics. It does not merely say every event has a cause in the narrow sense; it is broader, demanding a reason or ground for every fact, existence, and truth. And accepting it is not cost-free, since pushed hard it threatens to make everything necessary, so treating the principle as an obvious certainty, or as equivalent to simple causal determinism, misreads a contested thesis with deep and disputed consequences.
origin: Named and made central by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz as one of his two great principles alongside the principle of contradiction, with antecedents in Anaximander, Parmenides, and Spinoza; later treated at length in Schopenhauer's On the Fourfold Root.
